text: Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey, with its rings of carved T-shaped stone pillars, was built by hunter-gatherers around 9500 BCE, more than 6,000 years before Stonehenge was begun.
Napoleon was not unusually short. He measured 5 pieds 2 pouces in French units, about 1.68 m (5 ft 6 in), roughly average for his era; British cartoons and the longer French inch did the rest.

No horned helmet has ever been found from the Viking Age. The best-preserved Viking helmet, dug up at Gjermundbu in Norway in 1943, is a rounded iron cap; the horns come from costumes for Wagner's Ring in 1876.

Marie Antoinette almost certainly never said 'let them eat cake'. Rousseau's Confessions, written around 1765, credits the brioche line to an unnamed 'great princess', when she was a child of about nine in Austria.
When Mansa Musa of Mali passed through Cairo on pilgrimage in 1324, he spent and gave away so much gold that, according to al-Umari, its value there was still depressed about twelve years later.

Great Zimbabwe, the stone city that gave the modern country its name, was built by ancestors of the Shona from about the 11th century; colonial writers insisted Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba built it.
In the 3rd century CE the prophet Mani listed the four great kingdoms of the world as Persia, Rome, Aksum and (probably) China. Aksum, in today's Ethiopia and Eritrea, minted its own gold coins.

The Inca ran an Andean empire of millions without a conventional script, recording census and tribute on khipu, knotted strings. Their numbers can be read; whether some khipu also encoded words is unresolved.
In 1414 a giraffe from East Africa, acquired in Bengal by Zheng He's treasure fleet, reached the Ming court, where officials hailed it as a qilin, an auspicious creature of legend.

Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, founded as a mosque around 859 and traditionally credited to a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, is often cited as the oldest continuously operating institution of higher learning.
The Indus script of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro remains undeciphered: its inscriptions average about five signs, no bilingual text has been found, and the language behind it is unknown.
Russia's October Revolution happened in November by most of the world's reckoning. Russia still used the Julian calendar, so 25 October 1917 there was 7 November elsewhere; it switched in 1918.

In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis had Vienna doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and maternal deaths on his ward fell to about 1 to 2 percent. Colleagues largely rejected him; he died in an asylum in 1865.
The Antikythera mechanism, a Greek geared bronze device from roughly the 2nd century BCE, predicted eclipses. Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity is known for over a thousand years afterward.
The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is not Gutenberg's Bible but Jikji, a Korean Buddhist text printed in 1377, nearly 80 years earlier. Its only surviving volume is in Paris.

Magellan did not sail around the world: he was killed at Mactan in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the Victoria home to Spain in 1522 with 18 of the roughly 240 to 270 men who set out.
No one in the Byzantine Empire called it that. Its people called themselves Romans, and the label 'Byzantine' was popularized by German scholar Hieronymus Wolf in 1557, a century after its fall.
The 1815 eruption of Tambora in Indonesia cooled the globe, causing the 1816 'Year Without a Summer'. Kept indoors by storms at Lake Geneva that June, Mary Shelley began Frankenstein.
Japanese officer Hiroo Onoda kept up his guerrilla war on Lubang Island in the Philippines until 1974, refusing to surrender until his former commander flew in and formally rescinded his orders.

The word 'genocide' first appeared in print in 1944. Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin built it from Greek genos (people, race) and Latin -cide (killing); the UN Genocide Convention followed in 1948.
In 897 Pope Stephen VI had the body of Pope Formosus, dead about nine months, exhumed, robed and put on trial at the Cadaver Synod. The corpse was found guilty and thrown into the Tiber.
Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov showed in 1952 that Maya glyphs were partly phonetic, the key to their decipherment, working only from published copies. He first saw Maya ruins around 1990.
Sandy Island, shown in the Coral Sea on maps and Google Earth for decades, was 'undiscovered' in 2012 when an Australian research ship reached its position and found open ocean about 1,400 m deep.

The Mountains of Kong, a great range across West Africa, appeared on maps for nearly a century after 1798. They did not exist; French explorer Louis-Gustave Binger confirmed it on his 1887–89 expedition.

Hittite, language of a forgotten Bronze Age empire in Anatolia, was cracked in 1915 by Bedřich Hrozný after he read one line as 'you will eat bread and drink water'. It is the oldest attested Indo-European language.
On 18 November 1883 North American railroads replaced a patchwork of local times with standard time zones. Where clocks were set back at noon, people lived through the 'day of two noons'.

The Berlin Wall opened partly by mistake. On 9 November 1989 East German spokesman Günter Schabowski, asked when new travel rules applied, said 'immediately, without delay'; crowds headed for the border that night.

The Dutch tulip mania of 1637 was far milder than legend. Historian Anne Goldgar, working through the archives, found few people involved, minor economic effects and nobody she could show went bankrupt.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, first found by Bedouin shepherds at Qumran around 1947, include the oldest known Hebrew Bible manuscripts, about a thousand years older than the medieval copies used before.
"The past is a foreign country: they do things differently there." (L. P. Hartley, The Go-Between, 1953)
